questions.q: Why is hardcoding a real API key directly into a source file a serious problem, even if you delete that line in a later commit?
options: It isn't a problem as long as the file is eventually deleted
Once committed, the key remains in the repository's git history forever, retrievable even after the line is removed in a later commit
Git automatically encrypts any string that looks like an API key
Hardcoded keys only matter if the repo is public
questions.explain: git history preserves every past commit — deleting a line in a new commit doesn't erase it from earlier commits, so a committed secret stays recoverable from git log/git show.

options: It validates that every environment variable is well-formed
It reads the .env file and copies its key=value pairs into process.env at startup
It deletes the .env file after reading it
It encrypts the .env file
questions.explain: dotenv's job is purely to load — it reads .env once at startup and populates process.env so the rest of the app can read those values normally; it performs no validation.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a committed `.env.example` file alongside a gitignored `.env`?
options: It documents exactly which environment variable names the project expects, with real values left blank, so a new developer knows what to fill into their own .env
It's a backup copy of the real secrets in case .env is lost
It replaces the need for a .gitignore entry
It's required by Node.js to run any script
questions.explain: .env.example is committed and shows the expected variable names (with blank or placeholder values); .env itself holds the real secrets and must never be committed, which .gitignore enforces.

questions.q: After `dotenv` loads .env, what type does `process.env.RPC_URL` have, and why does this lesson pair dotenv with a zod schema?
options: It's already guaranteed to be a valid URL string by dotenv alone, so zod is redundant
It's still typed string | undefined — dotenv only loads the value into process.env, it doesn't validate it, which is exactly the gap a zod schema closes
dotenv converts it to a bigint automatically
process.env values are always typed as numbers
questions.explain: Loading and validating are two separate concerns: dotenv gets the string into process.env, but it's still string | undefined until something (like zod's .parse()) checks that it's actually present and well-formed.

questions.q: What is the role of `.gitignore` in this pattern?
options: It lists `.env` so the file containing real secrets is never accidentally committed to the repository
It tells dotenv which variables to load
It encrypts committed files automatically
It is only relevant for compiled JavaScript output, not .env files
questions.explain: .gitignore prevents git from tracking the listed paths — adding .env to it is what stops the file holding real secrets from being committed, even by someone who forgets the convention.
